```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 5)
REPO <- "Rayonier/Code_Profiling_Workshop"
# Lines of a file from the first match of `from` to the first later match of `to`.
code_lines <- function(file, from, to = NULL) {
  x <- readLines(file)
  i <- grep(from, x)[1]
  j <- if (is.null(to)) length(x) else i - 1 + grep(to, x[i:length(x)])[1]
  x[i:j]
}
```

```{r palette, include=FALSE}
library(ggplot2)
FOREST <- "#2E6B3F"; ORANGE <- "#D9661F"; NAVY <- "#33506E"
INK <- "#222222"; GREY <- "#B9B4AC"

ACT_LABELS <- c("MEASURE", "LOCATE", "ZOOM IN", "DECIDE")
ACT_SUB    <- c("how slow, really?", "which R call?", "which C++ line?", "what to fix first")
story_arc <- function(highlight) {
  n <- length(ACT_LABELS)
  df <- data.frame(x = seq_len(n), label = ACT_LABELS, sub = ACT_SUB,
                   is_now = seq_len(n) == highlight, done = seq_len(n) < highlight)
  df$fill <- ifelse(df$is_now, FOREST, ifelse(df$done, NAVY, GREY))
  arrows <- data.frame(x = head(df$x, -1) + 0.42, xend = tail(df$x, -1) - 0.42, y = 0, yend = 0)
  ggplot() +
    geom_segment(data = arrows, aes(x, y, xend = xend, yend = yend),
                 arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.18, "cm"), type = "closed"), color = GREY, linewidth = 0.8) +
    geom_tile(data = df, aes(x, 0, fill = fill), width = 0.85, height = 0.55, show.legend = FALSE) +
    geom_text(data = df, aes(x, 0.02, label = label), color = "white", fontface = "bold", size = 5) +
    geom_text(data = df, aes(x, -0.42, label = sub), color = INK, size = 4) +
    scale_fill_identity() + xlim(0.4, n + 0.6) + ylim(-0.65, 0.4) +
    theme_void() + theme(plot.background = element_rect(fill = "white", color = NA))
}
```

> **Where we left off.** In the lecture, we met a stand-projection script
> that grows a couple of thousand plantation plots forward 30 years and
> builds one summary table. It's slow, and everyone already "knows" why: the
> C++ growth model. The three ideas to carry forward:
>
> 1. **Your intuition about where time goes is usually wrong.** Measure first.
> 2. **Profile at two levels:** R tells you *which call* is slow; callgrind
>    tells you *which line inside the C++* is slow.
> 3. **Fix the biggest measured cost first.** Optimizing anything else is
>    premature.
>
> No valgrind or GitHub experience is needed: every step is given. If your
> cloud run fails or sits in the queue, the repository's `results` branch has
> identical pre-made output, so nothing later depends on your run. If GitHub
> isn't reachable at all, follow the **Plan B** boxes; the offline bundle has
> everything.

```{r arc-0, echo=FALSE, fig.height=1.6}
story_arc(1)
```

## 1. Setup + start the callgrind run (10 min)

**First, check your setup.** This chunk only *checks*; if anything is
missing, run `source("bootstrap.R")` once in the console, then come back.

```{r preflight}
need <- c("Rcpp", "profvis", "bench", "ggplot2")
miss <- need[!vapply(need, requireNamespace, logical(1), quietly = TRUE)]
if (length(miss)) stop("Missing packages: ", paste(miss, collapse = ", "),
                       ". Run source(\"bootstrap.R\") in the console, then re-run this chunk.")

  stop("data/trees.csv not found -- set the working directory to the workshop folder ",
       "(Session > Set Working Directory > To Source File Location).")
cat("Setup OK\n")
```

**Now start the callgrind run, before anything else.** It takes several
minutes on GitHub's machine, so it runs while you do sections 2 and 3:

1. Open **`github.com/`r REPO``** → the branch dropdown (it says `main`) →
   type a branch name (your username) → **Create branch from main**.
2. Go to the **Actions** tab → **Callgrind profile** → **Run workflow** →
   choose **your branch** and `version: naive` → **Run workflow**.
3. Leave that tab open and carry on here. You'll come back to it in section 4.

> **Plan B — can't reach GitHub?** Use the offline bundle from your invite
> email: unzip it and set it as your working directory. Skip steps 1–3. In
> section 4 you'll read the pre-generated callgrind output in `results/`,
> which is exactly what your run would have produced.

Load the code and data:

```{r load}
Rcpp::sourceCpp("src/grow.cpp")              # grow_plot(): the C++ growth model
source("R/project_stands.R", keep.source = TRUE)
trees <- read.csv("data/trees.csv")
plots <- read.csv("data/plots.csv")
cat(sprintf("%d plots, %d trees\n", nrow(plots), nrow(trees)))
```

The whole pipeline is one short R function. It's worth reading before you
measure it:

```{r show-pipeline, eval=FALSE, code=code_lines("R/project_stands.R", "^project_stands_slow", "^[}]")}
```

<details><summary><b>Under the hood:</b> the growth model and the data</summary>

`grow_plot()` (in `src/grow.cpp`) grows every tree on a plot in 5-year
steps, using published equations for loblolly pine from the **Southern
variant of the US Forest Service's Forest Vegetation Simulator** (FVS Staff
2008, revised 2026, *Southern (SN) Variant Overview*). These include
large-tree diameter growth, potential height growth from Carmean et
al. (1989) site curves, height-growth modifiers, bark ratio and background
mortality. The coefficients are listed in `src/fvs_sn_lp.h`, with equation
numbers.

It is a teaching re-implementation, not FVS. Crown ratio is held constant,
and there's no density-related mortality, so basal area runs high late in
the projection. The plots are **simulated**: tree heights come from the
published height–diameter and site-curve equations, everything else is
made up. None of that matters for profiling. What matters is that it's real
arithmetic, with real costs.

</details>

**Q1.1** Before you measure anything, write down:
(a) which part of `project_stands_slow()` you think takes the most time, and
(b) roughly what share of the total it takes. We'll come back to your guess
at the end.

## 2. Timing: is it actually slow, and how slow? (8 min)

Start with a stopwatch on the whole thing:

```{r time-slow}
t_slow <- system.time(res_slow <- project_stands_slow(trees, plots))
t_slow
```

> **Elapsed vs. user vs. system, in plain words.** *Elapsed* is wall-clock
> time, what you waited for. *User* is time the CPU spent running your code.
> *System* is time the operating system spent on your behalf (memory,
> files). When they disagree a lot, something other than computation is
> going on.

One run is weak evidence. Run it again and you'll get a slightly different
number, because other programs, the cache and memory all vary. For small
pieces of code, `bench::mark()` runs each one many times and reports the
spread. It also reports how much memory each one allocated.

Here are three things the loop does for **one plot**: pick out that plot's
trees, grow them, and stack the result onto an output table that already
holds most of the other plots:

```{r bench-pieces}
id  <- plots$PlotID[1]
pt  <- trees[trees$PlotID == id, ]
res <- grow_plot(pt$Dbh, pt$Ht, pt$CR, pt$TPA, plots$Age[1], plots$SI[1], 30)
big <- res_slow[seq_len(nrow(res_slow) - nrow(res)), ]   # the table near the end of the loop

pieces <- bench::mark(
  subset_trees = trees[trees$PlotID == id, ],
  grow_cpp     = grow_plot(pt$Dbh, pt$Ht, pt$CR, pt$TPA, plots$Age[1], plots$SI[1], 30),
  rbind_output = rbind(big, data.frame(PlotID = id, res)),
  check = FALSE, min_iterations = 20
)
pieces[, c("expression", "median", "mem_alloc")]
```

Now time **just the C++**: grow every plot, with the trees already split up
so no R table work is included.

```{r time-cpp}
rows <- split(seq_len(nrow(trees)), trees$PlotID)
grow_all <- function(grow) {
  for (k in seq_len(nrow(plots))) {
    i <- rows[[plots$PlotID[k]]]
    grow(trees$Dbh[i], trees$Ht[i], trees$CR[i], trees$TPA[i], plots$Age[k], plots$SI[k], 30)
  }
}
t_cpp <- system.time(grow_all(grow_plot))
t_cpp
cpp_share <- t_cpp[["elapsed"]] / t_slow[["elapsed"]]
```

On this machine, the C++ growth model is **`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * cpp_share)`**
of the pipeline's `r sprintf("%.1f", t_slow[["elapsed"]])` seconds.

**Q2.1** Run the `time-slow` chunk three times. How much does the elapsed
time vary? How big would a speedup have to be before you'd believe it from
one run of each version?

**Q2.2** Multiply each median in the `bench-pieces` table by the number of
plots (`r nrow(plots)`). Which piece adds up to the most? Does that match
your answer to Q1.1? Then look at `mem_alloc`: why would picking out about
200 trees allocate megabytes? *(Careful: `rbind_output` was measured near
the end of the loop, when the table is biggest. Early in the loop it's
cheap. Why?)*

## 3. Profiling from R (17 min)

```{r arc-3, echo=FALSE, fig.height=1.6}
story_arc(2)
```

Timing pieces one at a time only works when you already know which pieces
to time. A **profiler** finds them for you. R's built-in profiler is a
*sampling* profiler: every 20 ms it notes which function calls are running,
and at the end it counts how often each one showed up.

<details><summary><b>Under the hood:</b> sampling profilers</summary>

A function that shows up in 30% of the samples took about 30% of the time.
Sampling is cheap, so the program runs at nearly normal speed. But it's
statistical: anything much shorter than the sampling interval can be missed
entirely, and short runs give noisy profiles. To see *lines* rather than
just functions, R needs the source references that `keep.source = TRUE`
keeps (we used it in `source()` above).

</details>

### Base R: `Rprof()`

```{r rprof}
prof_file <- tempfile()
Rprof(prof_file, interval = 0.02, line.profiling = TRUE)
invisible(project_stands_slow(trees, plots))
Rprof(NULL)
prof <- summaryRprof(prof_file, lines = "show")
head(prof$by.self, 8)
```

Each row is one line of code: `project_stands.R#12` means line 12 of
`R/project_stands.R` (`file.show("R/project_stands.R")` to look). `self.pct`
is the share of all samples taken while that line was running. R's internal
helpers, like `[.data.frame` for subsetting, are counted against the line
that called them.

### Interactive: `profvis`

`profvis` runs the same profiler and draws the result. The **flame graph**
shows time left to right and the call stack bottom to top. A wide bar means
lots of time. Hover over a bar to see its line of code; click
**Data** for a table.

```{r profvis, fig.height=6}
profvis::profvis(project_stands_slow(trees, plots), height = "500px")
```

Look for `grow_plot` in the flame graph. It's one flat bar with nothing on
top. R can see that the C++ function was running, but not what it was doing
inside. That's the job of section 4.

**Q3.1** Which *line* of `project_stands_slow()` accounts for the most time?
Which accounts for the second most? Is either one the C++ call?

**Q3.2** The `rbind()` line looks harmless. Why does its total cost grow
*faster* than the number of plots? *(Hint: each time round the loop, what
does R have to copy to make the new, one-plot-longer table?)*

**Stretch (only if you're ahead).** Profile `project_stands_slow()` on the
first half of the plots (`plots[1:1000, ]`) and compare it with the full
run. Which bar roughly doubles, and which grows by more than that?

## 4. Inside the C++: callgrind on a Linux runner (20 min)

```{r arc-4, echo=FALSE, fig.height=1.6}
story_arc(3)
```

R's profiler stops at the C++ boundary. **Callgrind** (part of valgrind)
goes inside. It runs the program on a simulated processor and counts every
instruction each line executes. The counts are exact and come out the same
on every run, but the program runs 20–50× slower, and valgrind only runs on
Linux. That's why it runs on a GitHub Actions Linux machine.

### What the workflow did

Your run from section 1 should be finished by now. Open it from the
**Actions** tab. The top of the report is on the run's summary page, and the
full files are under **Artifacts** at the bottom. Here's what it ran, one
step at a time:

```{r show-workflow, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
cat("```yaml", code_lines(".github/workflows/callgrind.yml", "^jobs:"), "```", sep = "\n")
```

In plain words:

- **Set up R and install valgrind.** This gives a clean Linux machine with
  R, Rcpp and valgrind.
- **Compile with debug symbols.** `ci/Makevars` adds `-g` so callgrind can
  match instructions to source lines. It keeps `-O2` so the code is as
  optimized as a normal build.
- **Run under callgrind.** It runs `ci/profile_cpp.R`, which grows the first
  200 plots. `--instr-atstart=no` plus the `CALLGRIND_START/STOP_INSTRUMENTATION`
  markers in `grow.cpp` mean that only the growth loop is counted. R's own
  startup, the compiler and reading the CSV are left out.
- **Annotate.** `callgrind_annotate` turns the raw counts into two readable
  reports: per function (`annotate_inclusive_naive.txt`) and per source line
  (`annotate_naive.txt`).

> **Your run failed or is still queued?** Switch to the `results` branch on
> GitHub and open `results/annotate_naive.txt` there, or run
> `git fetch && git checkout origin/results -- results/`. It's identical
> output.
>
> **Plan B — offline?** Your `results/` folder already has everything. Read
> `.github/workflows/callgrind.yml` alongside the walkthrough above; it's what
> would have run.

### Reading the report

The unit is **Ir**, *instructions read* (executed). Two views matter:

- **Inclusive** cost: the instructions in a function *plus everything it
  calls*. `grow_plot` has almost 100% inclusive cost, because everything
  happens inside it.
- **Self** cost: the instructions in the function's own lines only. This is
  where the work actually happens.

```{r callgrind-helpers, include=FALSE}
annot_path <- function(version, kind = c("inclusive", "source")) {
  kind <- match.arg(kind)
  file.path("results", sprintf(if (kind == "inclusive") "annotate_inclusive_%s.txt"
                               else "annotate_%s.txt", version))
}
has_results <- file.exists(annot_path("naive"))
total_ir <- function(version) {
  p <- annot_path(version)
  if (!file.exists(p)) return(NA_real_)
  line <- grep("PROGRAM TOTALS", readLines(p), value = TRUE)[1]
  as.numeric(gsub(",", "", sub("^\\s*([0-9,]+).*", "\\1", line)))
}
```

```{r callgrind-top, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
if (has_results) {
  cat("Top of the inclusive report for the naive version:\n\n```\n")
  cat(head(readLines(annot_path("naive")), 40), sep = "\n")
  cat("\n```\n")
} else {
  cat("> **Results pending.** This page was built before the first callgrind run,",
      "so there's no report to show yet. Use the report from your own run",
      "(Actions tab) or from the `results` branch.\n")
}
```

And here is the part of the line-by-line report that covers the main loop in
`grow.cpp`. Each line shows its instruction count to the left of the code:

```{r callgrind-lines, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
if (has_results) {
  src <- readLines(annot_path("naive", "source"))
  hit <- grep("plot basal area in larger trees", src, fixed = TRUE)
  if (length(hit)) {
    cat("```\n"); cat(src[max(1, hit[1] - 6):min(length(src), hit[1] + 14)], sep = "\n"); cat("\n```\n")
  } else {
    cat("> Open `results/annotate_naive.txt` and search for `grow.cpp`.\n")
  }
} else {
  cat("> **Results pending** (see above).\n")
}
```

(a) a calculation that gives the same answer for every tree on a plot, but

(b) something that copies the tree data every cycle.

**Q4.4** Callgrind counts instructions, not seconds. Name something that

## 5. Reading the results side by side (12 min)

You now have two profiles that answer different questions:

| | R profiler (`profvis`) | callgrind |
|---|---|---|
| Measures | share of **wall time** | share of **instructions** |
| Sees | R calls and lines | C++ functions and lines |
| Inside C++? | no: one opaque bar | yes |
| Run to run | varies a little | identical |

They fit together like this. R's profile says how big the C++ box is, and
callgrind says what's inside the box. That makes it possible to work out
the best case for any fix *before* making it:

> **The ceiling on any speedup.** If a part takes a share *p* of the total
> time and you make it *s* times faster, the whole program gets
> 1 / ((1 − p) + p / s) times faster. Even if you make that part *infinitely*
> fast, you can't beat 1 / (1 − p).

<details><summary><b>Under the hood:</b> Amdahl's law</summary>

Call the original run time 1. The part you speed up takes *p* and the rest
takes 1 − *p*. After the fix, the part takes *p* / *s*, so the new total is
(1 − *p*) + *p* / *s*. Speedup is old time over new time. This is
**Amdahl's law** (1967). It's the reason the *size* of a cost matters more
than how ugly the code looks.

</details>

With this machine's numbers: the C++ is
`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * cpp_share)` of the pipeline, so even an infinitely
fast `grow_plot()` gives at most a
**`r sprintf("%.2f", 1 / (1 - cpp_share))`×** speedup.

**Common ways to misread a profile:**

- Reading *inclusive* cost as if it were *self* cost. `grow_plot` "takes
  100%", but that tells you nothing about which line to fix.
- Trusting a single timing run (Q2.1).
- Profiling a toy input. With 10 plots instead of 2,000, the `rbind()`
  problem nearly disappears, because its cost grows with the square of the
  number of plots.
- Treating instructions as time. A `pow()` call and an addition are both
  "instructions" to read, but not equally slow (Q4.4).

**Q5.1** Using your numbers from sections 2 and 3: if `grow_plot()` were
infinitely fast, what's the most the whole pipeline could speed up?

**Q5.2** Same question, but for the two R lines you found in Q3.1 together.

## 6. Capstone — Decide: what do you fix first? (13 min)

```{r arc-6, echo=FALSE, fig.height=1.6}
story_arc(4)
```

Look back at your guess in Q1.1. Here are the measurements.

**Fix the biggest measured cost first: the R side.** `project_stands_fast()`
makes two small changes. It splits the tree table *once* instead of scanning
all `r format(nrow(trees), big.mark = ",")` rows for every plot, and it
collects results in a list and binds them *once* at the end:

```{r show-fast, eval=FALSE, code=code_lines("R/project_stands.R", "^project_stands_fast", "^[}]")}
```

```{r time-fast-r}
t_fast_r <- system.time(res_fast_r <- project_stands_fast(trees, plots))
t_fast_r
all.equal(res_slow, res_fast_r)       # same answer
cpp_share_now <- t_cpp[["elapsed"]] / t_fast_r[["elapsed"]]
```

From `r sprintf("%.1f", t_slow[["elapsed"]])` s to
`r sprintf("%.1f", t_fast_r[["elapsed"]])` s, a
**`r sprintf("%.1f", t_slow[["elapsed"]] / t_fast_r[["elapsed"]])`×**
speedup from changing a few lines of R. The C++ didn't change at all, but
now it's **`r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * cpp_share_now)`** of the time.

**Now the C++ is worth optimizing.** This is the other half of Knuth's
sentence: *"…yet we should not pass up our opportunities in that critical
3%."* The profile now points at the C++, and callgrind has already told us
exactly where to look. `src/grow_fast.cpp` uses the same published
equations with the problems from Q4.2 and Q4.3 fixed:

```{r time-fast-cpp}
Rcpp::sourceCpp("src/grow_fast.cpp")         # grow_plot_fast(): same inputs, same output
t_both <- system.time(res_both <- project_stands_fast(trees, plots, grow = grow_plot_fast))
t_both
all.equal(res_fast_r, res_both, tolerance = 1e-10)
```

```{r capstone-chart, echo=FALSE, fig.height=3.2}
tt <- data.frame(
  version = factor(c("Original", "R fixed", "R + C++ fixed"),
                   levels = rev(c("Original", "R fixed", "R + C++ fixed"))),
  cpp = c(t_cpp[["elapsed"]], t_cpp[["elapsed"]],
          t_both[["elapsed"]] - (t_fast_r[["elapsed"]] - t_cpp[["elapsed"]])),
  total = c(t_slow[["elapsed"]], t_fast_r[["elapsed"]], t_both[["elapsed"]])
)
tt$r <- tt$total - tt$cpp
long <- rbind(data.frame(version = tt$version, part = "R side", sec = tt$r),
              data.frame(version = tt$version, part = "C++ growth model", sec = tt$cpp))
ggplot(long, aes(sec, version, fill = part)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("R side" = NAVY, "C++ growth model" = ORANGE)) +
  labs(x = "Elapsed seconds", y = NULL, fill = NULL,
       title = "Where the time went, before and after each fix") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13) + theme(legend.position = "top")
```

**Q6.1** What was the speedup from the R fix alone, and from the C++ fix
applied after it? What would the C++ fix *alone* have bought, applied to the
original pipeline? (Use Amdahl's law with your section-2 numbers.)

**Q6.2 (discussion)** A colleague says: *"I rewrote the whole thing in C++
and it's 2× faster."* What do you ask before agreeing it was the right move?

**Q6.3 (discussion)** When *is* it reasonable to optimize before profiling?

## Wrap-up

```{r arc-wrap, echo=FALSE, fig.height=1.6}
story_arc(4)
```

Start to finish: everyone knew the C++ was the problem. The stopwatch said
otherwise, R's profiler pointed at two lines of R, and fixing them gave the
biggest win. Only then was the C++ the biggest cost, and callgrind showed
exactly which lines to fix. Four steps, one rule every time: **measure, then
fix the biggest measured cost.** See `takeaways.html` for the one-page
version.
